goals: Describe the procurement cycle from need to payment, including three-way matching.
Group purchases with the Kraljic matrix: routine, leverage, bottleneck and strategic.
Choose a supplier with a weighted scoring matrix.
Compare quotations using total cost of ownership, not price alone.
Prepare for a negotiation using BATNA and a concession plan.
Manage supplier performance with scorecards, SLAs and regular reviews.

handout.intro: Buying is not just placing an order. This session follows the full procurement cycle, then shows how to choose suppliers well and build relationships that keep supply reliable.

steps: **Identify the need** – a department needs something (raw material, spare parts, packaging).
**Specify** – write exactly what, how many, by when and to what standard. Vague specifications cause wrong orders.
**Requisition** – an internal request, approved by a budget holder.
**Source** – use an existing contract, or send a request for quotation (RFQ) to several suppliers.
**Purchase order (PO)** – the legal commitment: item, quantity, price, delivery date, place and terms.
**Receive** – the warehouse checks quantity, condition and specification, and records a goods received note (GRN).
**Pay** – accounts match the invoice with the PO and the GRN before paying.

callout.title: Three-way matching
callout.text: Pay only when the **purchase order**, the **goods received note** and the **invoice** agree. This stops overpayment, double payment and fraud.

sections.h: 2. Not all purchases are equal: the Kraljic matrix

blocks.p: Group what you buy by two questions: **How much does it affect our profit?** and **How hard is it to get (supply risk)?**

head: Group
Profit impact / supply risk
Example
How to manage
rows: Keep it simple: catalogues, standing orders, cards
Use competition between suppliers to get the best price
A special spare part from one maker
Secure supply: safety stock, backup supplier, longer contract
A key ingredient or main component
Long-term partnership, shared plans, joint improvement

sections.h: 3. Choosing a supplier: the weighted scoring matrix

blocks.p: Common criteria: **quality, price, reliability, capacity and compliance** (legal, ethical, safety). Give each criterion a weight (total 100%), score each supplier 1–5, multiply and add.

Supplier A wins even though it is not the cheapest, because quality has the biggest weight. Check the facts behind the scores: samples, site visits, references from other customers. Remove suppliers early if they fail basic checks (no insurance, poor safety record).
The quoted price is only part of the cost. TCO adds everything it costs to buy and use the product.

list: **Freight and fees** – a supplier at 2.10 plus freight may cost more than one at 2.50 with free delivery.
**Payment terms** – paying in 60 days keeps cash in your business for two months.
**Lead time** – a slow supplier means more stock in your warehouse.
**Quality** – defects cost inspection, returns, rework and delays.
**Minimum order quantity** – a low price for a huge order may tie up cash in stock you do not need.

blocks.p: Compare suppliers in a table with one row per cost, in **money**, not words. Then note the things money cannot show, such as innovation or route risk.

list: **Prepare** – know your goals, your limits and what the supplier needs.
**BATNA** – your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you will do if this deal fails (another supplier, make it yourself, wait). A strong BATNA gives you confidence.
**Concession plan** – decide in advance what you can give and what you want back. Trade, do not give away.
**Opening offer** – realistic but ambitious, based on market data.
**Listen** – the supplier’s problems (raw material cost, capacity) show where a creative deal is possible.
**Close in writing** – summarise and confirm what was agreed by email the same day.

blocks.p: A supplier who sees a long-term relationship will often **prioritise your orders** when capacity is short, **warn you early** about problems and **suggest improvements**. During the disruptions of recent years, companies with strong supplier partnerships usually recovered faster.

Trust is built by **actions repeated over time**: the supplier delivers on time, and you pay on time. It must go **both ways**: if you ask suppliers to hold stock for you, offer volume commitments or longer contracts in return.

callout.title: Trust and contracts
callout.text: A contract sets the minimum. Trust decides whether both sides work far above it. You need both.

head: Measure
Example
Agree in writing
rows: When does the clock stop? Is 10:05 for a 10:00 slot late?
What counts as a defect, and how you test
Time to reply and to fix

blocks.p: Put these on a **supplier scorecard** and discuss it in a **regular review** (monthly or quarterly). Record actions, owners and dates, and check them at the next review.

list: **Service level agreement (SLA)** – the performance standard and what happens if it is missed (for example, 95% on time).
**Breaches** – match the response to the problem: a one-day delay needs a conversation, repeated defects need the formal remedies.
**Root cause** – a late delivery is a symptom; find the cause (capacity, raw materials, planning) with the supplier.
**Corrective action plan** – what will change, who owns it, by when, and how you will check it.
**Backup suppliers** – keep them real: place small orders and keep their approval up to date.
**Supplier development** – train or support a supplier so it improves.

terms.meaning: The full process of getting goods and services: from the need to payment.
terms.example: Specifying, sourcing, ordering, receiving and paying for packaging.

terms.meaning: The document that commits the buyer to buy: item, quantity, price, date, place, terms.
terms.example: PO 4512: 2,000 cartons at 1.20 each, delivered by 10 May.

terms.meaning: Request for quotation: the same request sent to several suppliers so their prices can be compared.
terms.example: An RFQ for 10,000 labels sent to three printers.

terms.meaning: The warehouse record of what actually arrived.
Checking the PO, the GRN and the invoice agree before paying.
terms.example: The invoice is for 2,000 cartons but the GRN shows 1,950, so payment is held.

terms.meaning: A grid that groups purchases by profit impact and supply risk: routine, leverage, bottleneck, strategic.
terms.example: A special spare part from one maker is a bottleneck item.

terms.meaning: A table that scores suppliers on weighted criteria to compare them fairly.
All the costs of buying and using a product, not only its price.
terms.example: Price + freight + inspection + defects − value of paying later.

terms.meaning: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: your plan if the negotiation fails.
terms.example: A second supplier ready to deliver in four weeks.

terms.meaning: A regular report of a supplier’s performance on agreed measures.
Service level agreement: the agreed performance standard and the remedy if it is missed.
terms.example: 95% of orders on time, or a 2% rebate.

terms.meaning: A written plan to fix a problem: action, owner, deadline, check.
terms.example: Supplier adds preventive maintenance; buyer checks the records monthly.

terms.meaning: Buying an item from only one supplier.
terms.example: All bottle caps come from one factory: a risk if it stops.

terms.meaning: Helping a supplier improve its capabilities.
terms.example: Training a supplier’s team in quality checks.

quiz.q: Accounts will pay an invoice only when it agrees with two other documents. Which two?
options: The purchase order and the goods received note
The packing list and the delivery note
quiz.why: Three-way matching compares the purchase order, the goods received note and the invoice.

quiz.q: A special spare part is cheap, but only one maker in the world sells it. In the Kraljic matrix it is…
quiz.why: Low profit impact but high supply risk = bottleneck. Secure supply with safety stock or a backup.

quiz.q: Weights: quality 50%, price 50%. Supplier X scores quality 4, price 2. What is its weighted total?
Why might the cheapest supplier not be the best choice?
options: Other costs such as freight, defects and long lead times can make the total cost higher
The law requires the second-cheapest supplier
quiz.why: Total cost of ownership includes freight, quality problems, holding cost from long lead times, and more.

options: The lowest price you will accept
What you will do if this negotiation fails
quiz.why: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: your walk-away plan.

quiz.q: In a negotiation, the supplier cannot lower the price but worries about volume. What is a good trade?
options: Offer a longer contract in exchange for a lower price
Accept the price with nothing in return
quiz.why: Trade a concession for a concession: volume security for a better price.

quiz.q: What should happen after a supplier receives its quarterly scorecard?
options: Nothing; it is just a report
A review meeting with agreed actions, owners and dates
The supplier is replaced at once
quiz.why: A scorecard is useful only when it leads to a discussion and actions that are checked next time.

quiz.q: A backup supplier has never received an order. Why is this a problem?
options: It may not perform when you really need it
quiz.why: Keep backups real with small regular orders and an up-to-date approval.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in a service level agreement (SLA)?
options: 95% of orders on time, with a rebate if missed
The colour of the delivery truck
quiz.why: An SLA states the measurable performance standard and the remedy.

quiz.q: A supplier is late again and again. What is the best first step?
options: Find the root cause together, then agree a corrective action plan
quiz.why: A delay is a symptom. Find and fix the cause, then check the fix works.

workbook.intro: Use the Supplier scoring matrix and Total cost of ownership tools if you want to check your numbers.

questions.prompt: Name one purchase for each Kraljic group (routine, leverage, bottleneck, strategic) for a company you know in Qatar. Say how you would manage each one.
questions.hint: Example: a hospital, a supermarket chain or a construction company.

questions.prompt: Weights: quality 40%, price 30%, reliability 30%. Supplier A: 4, 3, 5. Supplier B: 5, 2, 3. Calculate both weighted totals and say which supplier you choose and why.
questions.hint: Multiply each score by its weight, then add.

questions.prompt: Supplier X quotes 10.00 per unit with free delivery. Supplier Y quotes 9.20 per unit, plus 1,200 freight, for 2,000 units. Y also has a 3% defect rate; each defect costs 15. Which is cheaper in total? Show your working.
You must renew a contract with your main packaging supplier, who wants a 6% price increase. Plan the negotiation: your BATNA, your opening position and two concessions you could trade.
questions.hint: What could you give the supplier that costs you little?

questions.prompt: Design a simple supplier scorecard with four measures. For each one, write exactly how you will measure it.
Give one reason why a long-term supplier relationship can be better than always choosing the cheapest quote.
questions.hint: Think about what happens in a shortage.

How confident are you with today's topic?
